text:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) — FIR and escalation pathway:
Section 173: every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, given orally or electronically to an officer in charge of a police station, must be reduced to writing, read over to the informant, and signed by the informant; a copy of the information must be furnished free of cost. The Supreme Court in Lalita Kumari v. Government of U.P. (2014) 2 SCC 1 held (under the predecessor CrPC Section 154) that registration of an FIR is mandatory where the information discloses a cognizable offence — the principle carries to the BNSS regime.

metadata.title: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 — FIR registration and escalation

text:
Escalation if the station house officer refuses to register: (1) send the complaint in writing to the Superintendent of Police, who may investigate or direct investigation (see BNSS Section 175 — verify the current subsection); (2) approach the concerned Judicial Magistrate, who may order investigation under Section 175(3); (3) file a private complaint before the Magistrate; (4) in appropriate cases, approach the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution for a writ of mandamus.
Section 193 (replacing CrPC Section 200): examination of the complainant on oath in private complaints.
Preserve proof: carry a copy of the written complaint and dispatch receipts; demand the free FIR copy.

text:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) — offences relevant to money and fraud disputes:
Section 316 — criminal breach of trust (replacing IPC Section 406): whoever, being in any manner entrusted with property or with dominion over it, dishonestly misappropriates or converts it to their own use, or dishonestly uses or disposes of it in violation of a legal contract or express direction, commits criminal breach of trust.
Section 318 — cheating (replacing IPC Section 420): whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces them to deliver property or to consent to retention of property, or intentionally induces them to do or omit to do anything they would not do if not so deceived, commits cheating. Online payment frauds, fake sellers and investment scams are prosecuted under this provision together with the Information Technology Act, 2000.

metadata.title: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — cheating and breach of trust

text:
Related BNS provisions (verify numbering): forgery (formerly IPC 463-471), criminal intimidation (formerly IPC 503-506), and defamation as a civil-criminal matter.
A complaint to police/economic offences wing may cite these provisions where the facts disclose a cognizable offence; the complaint narrative should state facts chronologically rather than merely asserting legal conclusions.

Code on Wages, 2019 — key provisions:
The Code consolidates the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 into one code.
Section 5: timely payment of wages — wages are to be paid on or before the prescribed day; the Code removes the historical wage ceiling for wage-payment protection, extending timely-payment norms to all employments (subject to rules and enforcement by the appropriate government).
Section 17: the appropriate government appoints inspectors-cum-facilitators; Section 42 provides for penalties including fines for contravention of wage-payment obligations.

metadata.title: Code on Wages, 2019 — uniform wage payment standards

Important caveat: the Code has been enacted but is being brought into force in phases through Central and State notifications and rules. The classic statutes (Payment of Wages Act, 1936 and Industrial Disputes Act, 1947) continue to govern in the interim where the Code is not yet operative. Verify the current commencement position in your state before relying on it.

Consumer Protection Act, 2019 — key provisions:
Section 2(11) defines 'deficiency' as any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature or manner of performance of a service, or breach of an express or implied warranty.
Section 2(42): 'consumer' includes persons who buy goods or avail services, including online transactions (e-commerce buyers are expressly covered).
Section 35: a complaint may be filed by a consumer (or registered consumer association / Central or State authority) alleging defect in goods, deficiency in service, unfair trade practice, overcharging or hazardous goods.
Section 38-39: the commissions can direct removal of defects, replacement of goods, refund of price paid, compensation for loss, discontinuance of unfair practices, and compensation for hardship or mental agony caused to the consumer.

metadata.title: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 — remedies for defective goods and deficient services

text:
Section 69: limitation — a complaint must ordinarily be instituted within two years from the date on which the cause of action arose (extensions only on sufficient cause shown).
Complaints can be filed electronically through the e-Daakhil platform, and physical filing remains available. Fees for filing before the District Commission are prescribed in slabs by claim value (verify the current schedule before filing).

text:
Indian Contract Act, 1872 — key provisions for everyday disputes:
Section 10: agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not expressly declared void. A signed rental agreement, employment contract or service agreement is ordinarily a contract within this section.
Section 37: the parties to a contract must either perform or offer to perform their respective promises, unless performance is dispensed with or excused.
Section 73: when a contract has been broken, the party who suffers from the breach is entitled to receive compensation for any loss or damage naturally arising in the usual course of things from the breach. Compensation aims to restore the injured party, not to punish.

metadata.title: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — formation and breach

text:
Section 74: where a contract contains a stipulation for a penalty, only reasonable compensation can be recovered.
Application to security deposits: a landlord's obligation to refund a deposit arises from the tenancy agreement; wrongful withholding after the tenant has fulfilled obligations is actionable as breach of contract, and the tenant may recover the deposit with interest as compensation where proved.

text:
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 — key provisions:
Section 2(s): 'workman' means a person employed in an industry for hire or reward, excluding mainly managerial and supervisory roles. Whether a person is a workman is a jurisdictional fact — it determines access to industrial remedies.
Section 2A: discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination of an individual workman itself constitutes an industrial dispute, allowing the workman to raise the dispute directly.
Section 10/12: disputes may be referred to conciliation officers and (industrial tribunals/labour courts) by the appropriate government; conciliation through the labour department is a common first step for wage and termination disputes.

metadata.title: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 — recovery of dues by workmen

text:
Section 33C: where any money is due to a workman from an employer under a settlement, award or under the contract, the workman may apply to the appropriate government/labour court for recovery — a speedier recovery mechanism than a civil suit for workmen.
Practical pathway: (1) written demand; (2) approach the Labour Commissioner/Assistant Labour Commissioner for conciliation and, where applicable, a Section 33C application; (3) managerial staff outside the definition of workman may instead pursue a civil suit for salary under the employment contract.

Information Technology Act, 2000 — key cybercrime provisions:
Section 43 (civil liability) and Section 66 (criminal liability): unauthorized access to a computer, computer system or computer network; downloading/copying data without authorization; introducing viruses or damaging the system.
Section 66C — identity theft: fraudulent or dishonest use of the electronic signature, password or any other unique identification feature of any other person. Punishable with imprisonment up to three years and fine.
Section 66D — cheating by personation using a computer resource: cheating by any personation through communication device or computer resource, as is common in phishing, fake profiles, fake customer-care and investment scams. Punishable with imprisonment up to three years and fine.

metadata.title: Information Technology Act, 2000 — cybercrime provisions

text:
Reporting pathway: (1) immediately call the bank's fraud line and the national cybercrime helpline 1930 and request a transaction hold/freeze where possible; (2) file a complaint on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in), preserving transaction references (UTR/RRN), chat screenshots and account details; (3) approach the local police station or cyber cell with the printed complaint and evidence.
Compensation claims for unauthorized transactions additionally proceed through the bank's grievance redressal, the banking ombudsman framework of the RBI (verify current scheme details on the RBI portal), and the consumer commissions.

Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 — key provisions:
Section 12 — eligibility for free legal services includes: (a) members of Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes; (b) victims of trafficking or beggars; (c) women and children; (d) persons with disability; (e) persons in custody; (f) persons whose annual income does not exceed the ceiling prescribed by the State Government (commonly in the range of ₹3 lakh in several states — verify the current ceiling for your state); and other categories.
Institutions: the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA), State Legal Services Authorities (SLSAs), High Court Legal Services Committees, District Legal Services Authorities (DLSAs) and Taluk Legal Services Committees provide free legal advice, mediation and panel advocates.

metadata.title: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 — free legal aid and Lok Adalat

text:
Section 19: Lok Adalats are organised to settle disputes through compromise; they have the powers of a civil court for the purposes of summoning and evidence.
Section 21: an award of a Lok Adalat is deemed to be a decree of a civil court and is final and binding on all parties — no appeal lies (a fast, inexpensive settlement route for compoundable matters, cheque cases, maintenance and minor civil claims).
Front doors for a citizen: the DLSA office at the district court complex, NALSA's helpline 15100, and legal aid clinics.

text:
Model Tenancy Act, 2021 — key points:
The Act is a model law circulated by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs to balance landlord and tenant interests. It applies only in states that adopt and enact it; several states continue under older rent-control legislation (e.g., the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, or state-specific tenancy laws). This jurisdictional variance must be verified for the user's state.
Security deposit: under the Model Tenancy Act the security deposit is ordinarily capped at two months' rent for residential premises (and a higher amount for commercial premises), refundable within a short statutory window after vacating, after deducting arrears and damages as agreed in the written agreement.

metadata.title: Model Tenancy Act, 2021 — security deposit norms (model law)
metadata.authority: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, Government of India
metadata.jurisdiction: India (model law — adoption varies by state)

text:
The Act contemplates written tenancy agreements, a Rent Authority to adjudicate disputes (including deposit refunds and eviction on prescribed grounds), and penalties for wrongful withholding.
Practical pathway for a deposit dispute: (1) written demand with a reasonable period; (2) if unresolved, recourse under the applicable state rent law/Rent Authority where one exists; (3) otherwise, a civil suit for recovery based on the tenancy agreement and the Indian Contract Act, 1872.

text:
Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 — accident claims:
Section 166: applications for compensation arising from death or permanent disablement or injury in road accidents may be made to the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) having jurisdiction — by the injured person, or by the legal representatives of the deceased, or by the insurer. Claims can be made on both fault and structured (no-fault) bases.
Section 140: no-fault liability — in death or permanent disablement cases, compensation is payable irrespective of fault, on proof of the accident only.
Section 161: hit-and-run compensation scheme — where the vehicle cannot be identified, compensation is paid under the Solatium Fund, with enhanced amounts notified from time to time (verify current figures).

metadata.title: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 — accident compensation claims

text:
Insurance angle: claims against the vehicle's insurer proceed within the MACT; own-damage and claim-rejection disputes with insurers go through the insurer's grievance channel, the insurance ombudsman (where eligible) and consumer commissions.
Practical steps after an accident: obtain the FIR copy, medical records and bills, take photographs, note witness details, and file the MACT claim at the earliest (delay can raise limitation objections — the Act itself does not prescribe a simple universal period, so act promptly and consult a lawyer).

text:
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 — Section 138 (cheque bounce):
Where a cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by them for discharge of a debt or liability is returned by the bank unpaid — because of insufficiency of funds, or because it exceeds the arrangement — the drawer is punishable with imprisonment up to two years, or with fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both.
Statutory procedure (strictly time-bound; verify the current provisos at indiacode.nic.in):
1. The payee/holder must present the cheque within its validity period.
2. On dishonour, the bank issues a 'return memo'.
3. The holder must send a written demand notice to the drawer, ordinarily within 30 days of receiving the return-memo information of dishonour, calling upon the drawer to pay the cheque amount.
4. The drawer has 15 days from receipt of the notice to make payment.

metadata.title: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 — Section 138 cheque dishonour

text:
5. If unpaid, the holder may file a criminal complaint before the Magistrate/Metropolitan Magistrate, ordinarily within one month of the expiry of the 15-day period (extension possible on sufficient cause).
Evidence essentials: the original dishonoured cheque, the bank's return memo, proof of dispatch and delivery of the demand notice, and material showing the debt/liability. A parallel civil suit for recovery is also possible.

Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 — key provisions:
Section 2(n) defines sexual harassment to include unwelcome acts or behaviour (directly or by implication) — physical contact and advances, demand or request for sexual favours, sexually coloured remarks, showing pornography, or any other unwelcome physical, verbal or non-verbal conduct of sexual nature.
Section 4: every employer with ten or more employees must constitute an Internal Committee (IC), chaired by a senior woman employee. Workplaces without an IC requirement may approach the Local Committee constituted under the Act.

metadata.title: POSH Act, 2013 — workplace sexual harassment redressal
metadata.instrument: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013

text:
Section 9: an aggrieved woman may make a written complaint of sexual harassment to the IC within three months of the incident (with a further extension of up to three months for good reason; complaints may be filed by relatives where the aggrieved woman is unable).
Section 10: the IC may, at the request of the complainant, settle the matter through conciliation (monetary settlement not permitted as the basis).
Section 13: on completion of inquiry the IC makes findings and recommends action; employers must act on the recommendations, and interim reliefs (e.g. transfer or leave) can be granted during the inquiry.
Section 19: employer duties include dissemination of the policy, workshops, and assisting in evidence. Non-compliance attracts penalties.
Conduct amounting to criminal offences can additionally be reported to the police (helplines: 112 emergency; 1091 women helpline).

text:
Payment of Wages Act, 1936 — key provisions:
Section 3: the Act regulates payment of wages to persons employed in specified industries whose wages do not exceed the notified ceiling (historically revised from time to time — verify the current applicability ceiling; employees above the ceiling may need other remedies such as a civil suit for salary under the contract of employment or, for 'workmen', remedies under industrial law).
Section 5: responsibility for payment of wages — wages must be paid before the 7th day after the wage period ends (10th day for establishments employing fewer than 1,000 persons).
Unauthorized deductions are prohibited; authorized deductions are capped by the Act.

metadata.title: Payment of Wages Act, 1936 — timely payment of wages

text:
Section 15: the appropriate government appoints an authority (e.g., Labour Commissioner-cum-Registrar or designated officer) to hear claims of delayed or withheld wages; the authority can direct refund of deductions and payment of wages, with compensation for delayed payment in appropriate cases.
Practical pathway: an employee with unpaid wages may (1) send a written demand to the employer, (2) file a claim before the labour authority under this Act where applicable, and (3) for workmen, pursue recovery under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (Section 33C) or a reference through the labour department.

text:
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 — key provisions:
Section 3: 'domestic violence' includes physical, sexual, verbal, emotional and economic abuse against a woman by an adult male person in a domestic relationship (including husbands, partners, and relatives of the husband).
Section 4: any person who has reason to believe that domestic violence is being or is likely to be committed may inform the Protection Officer — third parties (neighbours, NGOs, relatives) can report.
Section 12: an aggrieved woman (or a Protection Officer on her behalf) may apply to the Magistrate for one or more reliefs under the Act. The Magistrate may grant interim and ex parte orders.
Section 17: the woman's right to reside in the shared household — she cannot be evicted except in accordance with law.

metadata.title: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
metadata.instrument: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005

text:
Sections 18-22: reliefs include protection orders (restraining the respondent from violence or communication), residence orders, monetary reliefs (maintenance and medical expenses), custody orders for children, and compensation for injuries. Breach of a protection order is separately punishable under Section 31.
Support infrastructure: Protection Officers appointed in each district, women's helplines (1091; 181 in several states), One Stop Centres, free legal aid through DLSA, and police (112) in emergencies.

Right to Information Act, 2005 — key provisions:
Section 2(f): 'information' includes records, documents, memos, e-mails, opinions, advices, press releases, circulars, contracts and material in any electronic form held by a public authority.
Section 6: a citizen who desires to obtain information shall make a request in writing or electronically to the Public Information Officer (PIO) of the concerned public authority, with the prescribed fee — no reason need be given.
Section 7: the PIO must respond as expeditiously as possible, and in any case within thirty days of receipt (forty-eight hours where the information concerns the life or liberty of a person).

metadata.title: Right to Information Act, 2005 — access to government records

text:
Section 19: if no reply is received or the applicant is aggrieved, a first appeal lies to the first appellate authority within the public authority (ordinarily within 30 days); a second appeal lies to the Central Information Commission (CIC) or State Information Commission (SIC) ordinarily within 90 days.
Section 18: complaints of, among other things, refusal to receive applications or failure to reply can be made directly to the Information Commission.
RTI is a low-cost, high-leverage tool in many disputes: obtaining file notings on delayed sanctions, police action-taken reports, municipal records and ownership details.

text:
Specific Relief Act, 1963 — key remedies:
Section 10: specific performance of a contract may, in the discretion of the court, be enforced when the act agreed to be done is such that compensation in money is not adequate. Applied to agreements for sale of property or unique goods.
Section 14: contracts that cannot be specifically enforced (e.g. involving personal skill or dependent on multiple supervisory acts).
Section 34: any person entitled to a legal character or right may institute a suit for declaration that he is so entitled.
Section 38: perpetual injunctions may be granted to prevent breach of an obligation existing in favour of the plaintiff — used to stop dispossession, encroachment, publication of defamatory content, etc.

metadata.title: Specific Relief Act, 1963 — specific relief and recovery

text:
For money claims (unpaid deposits, unpaid dues), the ordinary remedy is a suit for recovery in a civil court of competent pecuniary jurisdiction; specific performance is generally for non-monetary obligations. Recovery suits are subject to the Limitation Act, 1963 (commonly a three-year period for simple contract claims — verify the applicable article on the facts).

text:
Transfer of Property Act, 1882 — key concepts:
Section 5: 'transfer of property' means an act by which a living person conveys property to one or more other living persons. Section 8: unless a different intention is expressed, a transfer passes to the transferee all the transferor's interest in the property.
Section 10: a condition absolutely restraining the transferee from alienating property is void.
Section 41: a person who acquires immovable property in good faith for consideration from a person with an apparently valid title is protected (the 'shelter' principle relevant to double-sale disputes).
Section 54: 'sale' of tangible immovable property of value above the threshold requires a registered instrument; agreements to sell are distinct from sales.

metadata.title: Transfer of Property Act, 1882 — transfers of immovable property

text:
Section 105: a lease of immovable property is a transfer of a right to enjoy the property for a certain time in consideration of rent; leases above one year ordinarily require registered instruments. Rent receipts and mutation records are primary documents proving tenancy/payment.

text:
Article 14 of the Constitution of India provides that the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.

Practical significance: arbitrary action by a public authority — for example, unreasoned refusal of a licence, discriminatory treatment by a government office, or arbitrary inaction on a legitimate complaint — can be challenged as violative of Article 14 before the High Court under Article 226 (or the Supreme Court under Article 32 where a fundamental right is directly involved).

Article 14 applies to 'State' action; purely private disputes are generally addressed through ordinary civil, criminal or consumer remedies rather than constitutional writs.

text:
Article 21 of the Constitution of India states that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.
Through judicial interpretation, Article 21 embraces the right to live with human dignity, the right to livelihood, protection against cruel and degrading treatment, and fair procedure before deprivation of liberty. It is central to habeas corpus petitions (against unlawful detention), challenges to custodial violence, and petitions protecting victims of violence or harassment where state protection is sought.
Where personal liberty is at immediate risk, the appropriate urgent remedies are approaching the nearest police, the High Court (writ jurisdiction), or the National/State Legal Services Authority for free urgent legal aid.

text:
Article 226 of the Constitution of India empowers every High Court to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases any Government, directions, orders or writs — including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto — for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose.
Because the power extends to 'any other purpose', a writ petition under Article 226 is a standard remedy against: refusal or inaction of a public authority (mandamus), unlawful detention (habeas corpus), quashing of illegal orders (certiorari), and arbitrary administrative action read with Article 14.

text:
Article 300A of the Constitution of India states that no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law. After the Forty-fourth Amendment, the right to property ceased to be a fundamental right but remains a constitutional right.

Practical significance: a person dispossessed of property otherwise than in accordance with law — whether by a private party or a state authority — may seek recovery of possession through civil courts, and in appropriate cases specific relief under the Specific Relief Act, 1963. Dispossession without legal authority is actionable.

text:
Article 32 of the Constitution of India confers on the Supreme Court the power to issue directions, orders or writs — including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto — which may be appropriate for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III (fundamental rights). The right to move the Supreme Court is itself guaranteed as a fundamental right.

Practical note: for most citizens' grievances, the High Court under Article 226 is the more accessible constitutional forum because it is geographically nearer and its writ power extends beyond fundamental rights. Article 32 petitions are generally reserved for direct violations of fundamental rights.

text:
Article 39A of the Constitution of India provides that the State shall secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice, on a basis of equal opportunity, and shall, in particular, provide free legal aid, by suitable legislation or schemes or in any other way, to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities.
This directive principle is implemented through the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987: the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA), State Legal Services Authorities (SLSAs) and District Legal Services Authorities (DLSAs) provide free legal advice, panel lawyers and, in eligible cases, free representation. The NALSA helpline is 15100.
Any litigant who cannot afford a lawyer should approach the DLSA at the district court complex.

text:
Practical note on civil recovery suits (demo guidance, not legal advice):
Forum: suits for recovery of money are filed before the civil court (or court of small causes / commercial court as applicable) whose pecuniary jurisdiction covers the claim value. Territorial jurisdiction commonly follows residence of defendant or cause of action — verify with local rules.
Pre-suit step: a written demand (legal notice) is customary and, for claims against the government, statutorily required (notice under the applicable state/Central enactment before suing public authorities — verify the notice period for your state).
Limitation: the Limitation Act, 1963 prescribes periods for different claims — commonly three years for simple contract-based recovery from when the breach/cause arises (verify the applicable article and any acknowledgements that reset limitation).

metadata.title: Civil courts and recovery suits — practical filing note

text:
Costs and procedure: court fees are set by state schedules scaled to claim value; pleadings should state facts chronologically with documents exhibited; execution of the decree is a separate stage after judgment.
Alternatives: mediation (including court-annexed and NALSA pre-litigation mediation), arbitration where the contract provides it, and Lok Adalat for compromise-friendly claims.

text:
Emergency helplines (India):
112 — pan-India emergency response number for police, fire and medical emergencies. In situations involving threats to life, violence, stalking, accidents or unlawful detention, calling 112 is the first step; documentation and legal processes follow.
1091 — women's helpline for harassment, domestic violence and distress; many states also operate 181 as a women & child welfare helpline. One Stop Centres provide medical, police and legal assistance at one place.
1098 — CHILDLINE for children in distress.
1930 — cyber financial fraud helpline (with cybercrime.gov.in for filing).
15100 — NALSA legal aid helpline for free legal advice.

text:
Labour department pathway for wage/employment grievances:
Where an employer withholds wages or dues, the employee may approach the office of the Labour Commissioner / Assistant Labour Commissioner (ALC) of the area: (i) officials verify the employment and dues; (ii) conciliation meetings between employer and employee are convened (the Industrial Disputes Act machinery); (iii) where a workman's money is due under a settlement/award/contract, a Section 33C IDA recovery application may be made; (iv) claims under the Payment of Wages Act are entertained by the notified authority.
Related central machinery: EPFO for provident fund dues (epfindia.gov.in), ESIC for employees' state insurance, and the Employees' Compensation Act machinery for workplace injuries. Grievances can also be lodged on the centralised CPGRAMS portal and the labour ministry's Shram Suvidha portal.

text:
NALSA — National Legal Services Authority (nalsa.gov.in, helpline 15100):
Free legal services available: legal advice, drafting support, panel advocates for litigation in courts/tribunals, and mediation through Legal Services Authorities at national (NALSA), state (SLSA) and district (DLSA) levels.
Eligibility (Section 12, Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987) includes women, children, SC/ST members, victims of trafficking, persons with disability, persons in custody, and persons below the income ceiling notified by the state (commonly around ₹3 lakh per annum in several states — verify your state's ceiling).
Lok Adalats: organised periodically by the authorities; awards are deemed civil court decrees and final. Pre-litigation mediation is encouraged for compoundable disputes (cheque cases, minor civil claims, maintenance).

text:
National Consumer Helpline (NCH) — 1915 / consumerhelpline.gov.in (INGRAM portal):
The Department of Consumer Affairs operates the National Consumer Helpline to register consumer grievances against sellers, e-commerce platforms and service providers. A consumer can call 1915 (or register on the portal) and receive a unique docket number; the grievance is forwarded to the company or to the relevant regulator or ombudsman for response.
Many e-commerce and banking disputes resolve at this stage because companies are incentivised to respond to NCH dockets. Registering a grievance also creates a dated record useful later before the consumer commissions.
When it does not work: escalate to a formal complaint on e-Daakhil before the District/State Commission under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, citing the docket and correspondence as evidence of attempted resolution.

text:
National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (NCRP) — cybercrime.gov.in; helpline 1930:
For online financial fraud (UPI scams, phishing, fake apps, unauthorised electronic transactions), speed matters: (1) call the bank's fraud helpline and 1930 immediately — the citizen financial cyber fraud helpline coordinates freezing of remaining funds through the banking system; (2) file a complaint on cybercrime.gov.in (report other cybercrime or women/child-related cybercrime categories; anonymous reporting is allowed for women/child-related complaints); (3) the complaint is routed to the concerned state police cyber cell, which may contact the complainant for statements and documents.
Preserve and attach: transaction IDs (UTR/RRN), account numbers of beneficiary, date-time, device details, chat screenshots, ads/links, and any call recordings.

For follow-up, the local police station or the district cyber cell can be approached with a printed copy of the NCRP complaint and evidence. Compensation for unauthorised electronic transactions also proceeds through bank grievance redressal, the RBI-integrated ombudsman scheme (verify current framework) and consumer commissions.

text: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal, (1997) 1 SCC 416 (Supreme Court of India):

metadata.title: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) 1 SCC 416

text: The Court issued binding requirements to be followed in all cases of arrest and detention, including: (i) police personnel carrying clear identification and name tags; (ii) a memo of arrest prepared and attested by a witness and countersigned by the arrestee, with the time and place of arrest; (iii) a friend or relative of the arrestee informed of the arrest and place of detention as soon as practicable; (iv) information about the arrest and detention displayed at a conspicuous place in the police station and in the district control room; (v) entry in the police register about the person informed; (vi) the arrestee entitled to meet his lawyer during interrogation, though not throughout; (vii) medical examination of the arrestee every 48 hours and documentation of injuries; (viii) copies of all documents including the arrest memo sent to the Magistrate.

metadata.title: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) 1 SCC 416

text:
Failure to comply renders the official liable for departmental action and contempt, and can support compensation claims and habeas corpus petitions under Articles 32/226 of the Constitution.
Relevance: the touchstone authority for rights upon arrest/detention; essential knowledge for unlawful-detention emergencies (alongside immediate remedies: police control room, High Court, NALSA 15100).

text:
Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh, (2014) 2 SCC 1 (Constitution Bench, Supreme Court of India):
Holding: if the information given to the police discloses the commission of a cognizable offence, its registration (First Information Report under Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973) is mandatory, and the police officer has no discretion to investigate first and register later. A preliminary inquiry may be conducted only in limited categories (e.g. matrimonial disputes, commercial offences, medical negligence, corruption cases where the allegation requires verification) solely to ascertain whether a cognizable offence is disclosed.

metadata.title: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh (2014) 2 SCC 1

text:
Directions issued include: (i) FIR registration followed by prompt investigation; (ii) a copy of the FIR to be given free of cost; (iii) action against officers who refuse to register without justification; (iv) remedies for the informant including approaching the Superintendent of Police under Section 154(3) CrPC and thereafter the Magistrate.
Relevance today: the successor provision in the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Section 173) embodies the same registration obligation; the judgment is the primary authority a citizen can cite when a police station declines to register a complaint disclosing a cognizable offence.

text:
Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta, (1994) 1 SCC 243 (Supreme Court of India):
Context: a flat allottee faced prolonged delay and deficiency by the Lucknow Development Authority; the question was whether the consumer fora could award compensation for harassment and mental agony.
Holding: service provided by a statutory authority like a development authority is 'service' under the Consumer Protection Act, and a consumer subjected to deficiency in service is entitled not only to refund of excess payments but also to compensation for harassment, mental agony and oppression. The Court directed that compensation should ordinarily be recovered personally from officials responsible for the harassment, to instil accountability in public administration.

text:
Sarla Verma (Smt.) & Ors. v. DTC & Anr., (2009) 6 SCC 121 (Supreme Court of India):
The Court restated the method for calculating compensation under the Motor Vehicles Act in death cases: (i) ascertain the deceased's income; (ii) deduct an amount towards the deceased's personal living expenses (the balance being the dependency of the family); (iii) multiply the annual dependency by a multiplier selected according to the age of the deceased (with the age of the deceased, not the claimants, being the relevant criterion, capped in the table); (iv) add conventional amounts for loss of consortium, funeral expenses and loss of estate.
The judgment harmonised widely varying MACT awards and remains the starting point for assessing fair compensation, subject to later refinements (e.g. National Insurance Co. v. Pranay Sethi (2017) — verify current position before computing a claim).

Consumer Protection (Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions) Rules, 2020 — procedure highlights:
Complaint contents: the complaint should set out the facts, the deficiency alleged, the relief sought, and be accompanied by evidence (invoice, warranty, correspondence) and an affidavit verifying the facts.
On admission, the commission issues notice to the opposite party; the opposite party must submit a written version within the time allowed (commonly 30 days, extendable as per the rules) and may deny or justify the deficiency.
Evidence of parties is ordinarily by affidavit; the commission may allow cross-examination where required. Commissions are empowered to order interim relief in appropriate cases.
E-filing: complaints, replies, and documents can be filed through the e-Daakhil portal including from locations outside the commission's territorial limits as permitted under the Act.

Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021 — pecuniary jurisdiction:
District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission: complaints where the value of goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed ₹50 lakh.
State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission: complaints where the consideration exceeds ₹50 lakh but does not exceed ₹2 crore.
National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission: complaints where the consideration exceeds ₹2 crore.
'Value' for jurisdiction is determined as prescribed under the 2019 Act and these rules (verify the current position — slabs have been revised in the past). Appeals from the District Commission lie to the State Commission within the limitation period prescribed by the Act, and from the State Commission to the National Commission.

text:
Right to Information (Regulation of Fee and Cost) Rules, 2012 — fees and costs for Central public authorities:
Rule 3: a request for information under Section 6(1) of the RTI Act must be accompanied by an application fee of rupees ten (₹10), payable by Indian Postal Order or demand draft or banker's cheque payable to the Accounts Officer of the public authority, or in cash against proper receipt, or through online payment where available (rtionline.gov.in accepts online payment).
Rule 4: further charges — rupees two (₹2) for each page in A4 or smaller; actual charge for larger copies; rupees fifty (₹50) per diskette/floppy; reasonable charges for samples/models; and rupees five (₹5) per hour of inspection after the first hour (free).
